desc: Tongue-in-cheek revival of 70s and 80s arena rock, led by Justin Hawkins' soaring falsetto.
Debut of scrappy Southern garage rock from three brothers and a cousin, with drawled, slurred vocals.
Bassless New York garage-punk debut, swinging from Karen O's feral yelps to the ballad Maps.
Jazz-inflected debut mixing torch-singer phrasing with hip hop beats and frank, witty North London attitude.
Hook-heavy debut produced largely by Dr. Dre and Eminem, featuring the club hit In da Club.
Double album split between Big Boi's funky Southern rap and André 3000's jazz-pop love songs.
Bass-and-drums duo playing frantic, high-volume noise rock with distorted, buried vocals.
Teenage Dizzee Rascal's skeletal, jagged debut that brought East London grime to wide attention.
Radiohead blend their guitar band roots with electronic textures on a tense, politically tinged record.
Pharrell's group mixes live rock instrumentation with funk and hip hop on its second album.
Shambolic, intimate garage rock charting the fraying friendship of Pete Doherty and Carl Barât.
Cee Lo's eclectic second solo album mixing gospel-tinged soul singing with funk and Southern rap.
Abrasive, swaggering Los Angeles rock drawing on the Stooges and post-punk noise.
Rock opera following a disaffected suburban youth, framed as a critique of post-9/11 America.
Flamboyant disco and glam pop debut, including a falsetto disco cover of Comfortably Numb.
Hushed, homespun acoustic songs with wobbly vocals, a defining record of the freak-folk scene.
Mike Skinner's narrative concept album about lost money, a relationship and everyday British life.
Looser, wilder follow-up of wiry guitar riffs and Caleb Followill's slurred tales of excess.
Bedroom-produced dance album built from 80s soft rock and pop samples, including In My Arms.
The Beta Band's final album, tighter and more song-focused while keeping its psychedelic collage approach.
Debut built on sped-up soul samples, mixing humour, faith and critique of education and consumerism.
Liverpool band's debut of saxophone-driven, offbeat indie rock with 60s and soul influences.
Morrissey's comeback album after seven years, with lush rock arrangements and sardonic, political lyrics.
Double album pairing raucous gospel-choir rock with gentler, mythic love songs.
Brian Wilson finally completes the abandoned 1967 Beach Boys project as a continuous suite.
Concept album about witchcraft and folklore built on pounding drums, chants and abrasive noise.
Companion to Want One, with operatic, darker chamber pop arrangements around Wainwright's voice.
Los Angeles collective blending hip hop, Latin, Middle Eastern and funk rhythms with political lyrics.
Debut combining layered doo-wop-inspired vocals with droning guitar loops and programmed beats.
Debut of angular, danceable guitar rock, featuring the hit Take Me Out.
Debut shaped by family deaths, building cathartic, communal anthems from strings and crashing guitars.
Album built almost entirely from human voices, including choirs, throat singing and beatboxers.
Debut of 80s-inspired synth rock with big choruses, including Mr. Brightside and Somebody Told Me.
The duo shift towards piano, marimba and acoustic textures while keeping bursts of blues guitar.
Beck reunites with the Dust Brothers for a sample-heavy mix of rock, hip hop and Latin flavours.
Lush, orchestrated baritone ballads about loneliness and love, named after a Sheffield meeting spot.
Debut mixing cheap-sounding electro beats, dancehall and baile funk with politically charged lyrics.
Concept album about Illinois history and people, with intricate orchestral arrangements and quiet confessional songs.
Common's album produced mainly by Kanye West and J Dilla, built on warm soul samples.
Antony's tremulous vibrato over piano and strings in songs about gender identity and mortality.
Breakup album recreating 60s girl-group soul with Mark Ronson and the Dap-Kings, including Rehab.
Double album paying tribute to 1920s-40s jazz, blues and soul, mixing vintage sounds with modern production.
Lyrically dense debut tackling street life, faith and the music industry, including Kick, Push.
Wu-Tang member's crime-saga album, packed with vivid storytelling over soul-sampling beats.
Ali Farka Touré's final album of hypnotic, blues-like guitar and ngoni from northern Mali.
Bombastic mix of space rock, electronica and prog, including Knights of Cydonia and Supermassive Black Hole.
Five long harp-led songs with Van Dyke Parks orchestral arrangements and dense, storybook lyrics.
Fast-selling debut of wiry guitar rock and sharp observations of Northern English nightlife.
Debut mixing punky indie rock with rave sirens and sci-fi literary references.
James Murphy's long, building dance tracks mixing disco, punk and ageing, including All My Friends.
Warm, intimate album first released as a pay-what-you-want download.
Darker follow-up recorded partly in a church, with pipe organ and themes of fear and faith.
Recorded across several countries, blending global rhythms with hip hop, including Paper Planes.
Damon Albarn supergroup with Paul Simonon, Tony Allen and Simon Tong, portraying a gloomy London.
Distorted, compressed electro-house debut including D.A.N.C.E. and Genesis.
Q-Tip's warm, jazzy solo comeback with live instrumentation and soulful grooves.
Kings of Leon move to polished stadium rock with Sex on Fire and Use Somebody.
Debut of reverb-drenched, layered harmonies and pastoral folk-rock.
Alex Turner and Miles Kane's side project, with sweeping 60s-style orchestral pop arrangements.
Mercury Prize-winning album of gentle, orchestral rock and Guy Garvey's Mancunian storytelling, including One Day Like This.
Comeback after eleven years, swapping trip hop for harsher krautrock rhythms and harsh electronics.
Debut of psychedelic synth-pop including Time to Pretend, Kids and Electric Feel.
Goldfrapp trade glam electro for soft, pastoral acoustic and electronic textures.
Funkier, brighter album mixing art rock with funk, horns and electronic beats.
Heavy album mixing brutal metal with more melodic, clean-sung tracks like Snuff.
Album known for Hayden Thorpe's falsetto, shimmering guitars and themes of masculinity and desire.
Sparse, slow songs with Callahan's deep baritone and orchestral touches about nature and solitude.
Washes of sample loops, deep bass and Beach Boys-style harmonies, including My Girls.
Intricately arranged chamber pop with close harmonies, including Two Weeks.
The band shift to synths and dance beats, including Zero and Heads Will Roll.
Knotty guitar lines and hocketing female harmonies, including Stillness Is the Move.
Sparse, whispered boy-girl duets over minimal guitar, bass and beats; Mercury Prize winner.
Karin Dreijer's solo debut of slow, chilly electronics and pitch-shifted vocals.
Hazy, swooning dream pop with Victoria Legrand's smoky vocals and shimmering organ.
Duo's soulful blues rock recorded at Muscle Shoals, including Tighten Up and Howlin' for You.
Lavishly produced album on fame and excess, including Runaway and Power.
Debut solo album backed by Midlake, with darkly funny songs about sexuality and self-loathing.
Concept album about an android messiah, mixing funk, soul, rock and orchestral passages.
Lush, anxious indie rock with Matt Berninger's baritone, including Bloodbuzz Ohio.
Hazy, warm guitar pop about memory and youth, including Helicopter and Desire Lines.
Grammy-winning concept album about suburban childhood and sprawl.
Breakup album including Rolling in the Deep and Someone Like You; a global best-seller.
Autoharp-led songs about war, focused on Gallipoli and English identity; Mercury Prize winner.
Busy, jammy rock with twin guitars, shifting rhythms and nods to prog and soul.
Concept album about a teenage day in Compton, framed with voicemail skits.
Warm, optimistic synth-pop dance tracks with tender lyrics about love.
Debut studio album of narrative R&B including Thinkin Bout You and Pyramids.
Jack White's solo debut of piano-tinged blues rock, including Sixteen Saltines and Love Interruption.
Debut mixing surf twang, 60s harmonies, electronic beats and percussive grooves.
Self-released comeback twenty-two years after Loveless, with blurred guitar and drum-and-bass touches.
Stark, abrasive record with distorted industrial synths and minimalist production, partly via Rick Rubin.
Surprise comeback after a decade away, with guitar rock and nods to his Berlin era.
Debut of bright, punchy synth-pop with Lauren Mayberry's clear vocals, including The Mother We Share.
Surprise-released visual album exploring sexuality and marriage, including Drunk in Love.
Swift's full move from country to 80s-inspired synth-pop, including Shake It Off and Blank Space.
Debut pairing airy falsetto with sparse, glitchy electronic production, including Two Weeks.
Long, propulsive songs mixing Springsteen-style rock with hazy, ambient textures and anxiety.
Reflective album about ageing and regret, opening with the global hit Hello.
Breakup album with string arrangements and electronic beats co-produced with Arca.
Dense album fusing jazz, funk and spoken word to explore race and fame, including Alright.
Debut by northern Malian exiles mixing desert blues guitar with garage rock energy.
Self-released grime album from Tottenham; Mercury Prize winner, including Shutdown.
Soft, spacious R&B about Black identity and self-care, with spoken interludes, including Cranes in the Sky.
Bowie's final album, made with a New York jazz band and released two days before his death.
Cohen's final album, a meditation on death produced by his son Adam.
Brighter third album shaped by Jamie xx's sample-based production, including On Hold.
Krautrock-inspired psychedelic pop with motorik rhythms and analog synths.
Reunion album exploring ageing and loss, with long post-punk and electronic tracks.
Coming-of-age album set over a house party, co-produced by Jack Antonoff, including Green Light.
Humorous, short songs blending jazz fusion, soft rock and funk, featuring Michael McDonald and Kenny Loggins.
Debut album of futuristic R&B with club-influenced electronic production about breakups and independence.
Debut album of candid R&B about insecurity and relationships, including The Weekend and Love Galore.
Leeds band moves from noisy psych rock to propulsive synth-driven songs about grief.
80s-inspired synth-funk album exploring gender and desire, released in French and English.
Country album with disco and soft rock touches; Grammy Album of the Year.
Little Simz's punchy album produced by Inflo, mixing boastful rap and vulnerable reflection.
Psychedelic soul album exploring identity and protest; produced by Danger Mouse and Inflo; Mercury Prize winner.
Ambient synth hymns about loss, grief and transcendence.
Home-recorded album built on percussion, found sounds and piano, exploring abuse and freedom.
Anonymous collective's album of soul, gospel and Afrobeat-tinged tracks about Black identity.
Companion to Folklore, made with Aaron Dessner, with narrative indie folk.
Soft, folk-leaning album about fame and escape, made with Jack Antonoff.
Short concept album alternating songs with spoken interludes from women about sex and relationships.
Noisier, denser album blending jangle pop with shoegaze fuzz.
London duo's heavy album blending rock, punk and electronic bass sounds.
First album of original Stones songs in eighteen years, produced by Andrew Watt.
Psychedelic big beat album with guest vocals from Beck and Halle Thomas.
Self-produced album of heavy guitars and synths exploring life and death.
First album of new Cure songs in sixteen years, long and slow-building, about loss.
Club-focused album of abrasive electronic pop, including 360 and Von Dutch.
Album made with Finneas, including Birds of a Feather.
Debut album of gentle, confessional indie folk songs.
Analog-synth electronic pop from the Colombian producer and singer.
Folk album from the Liberian-born, American-raised singer-songwriter.
Album from Poppy, known for mixing heavy metal with pop melodies.
Charli xcx songs written for the film adaptation of Wuthering Heights.
